claim: More than 6000 publications a year contain the term 'neuroimaging' on PubMed.
source: Each year, thousands of brain-imaging studies explore the links between brain and behavior: more than 6000 publications a year contain the term 'neuroimaging' on PubMed.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of publications containing a specific term in PubMed, which can be verified through database queries.

claim: Individual brain-imaging studies seldom have enough statistical power to establish fully trustworthy results.
source: Finding consistent trends in the knowledge acquired across these studies is crucial, as individual studies by themselves seldom have enough statistical power to establish fully trustworthy results (Button et al., 2013; Poldrack et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Button et al., 2013 and Poldrack et al., 2017.

claim: Only 30% of the terms contained in a neuroscience ontology or meta-analysis tool are common to another.
source: Indeed, only 30% of the terms contained in a neuroscience ontology or meta-analysis tool are common to another (see Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1, which shows vocabulary overlap between different neuroscience resources.

claim: Current meta-analysis approaches model all studies as asking the same question.
source: Yet, current meta-analysis approaches model all studies as asking the same question.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing meta-analysis methods based on the authors' understanding of the field.

claim: NeuroQuery captures the relationships and neural correlates of 7547 neuroscience terms across 13,459 neuroimaging publications.
source: We capture the relationships and neural correlates of 7547 neuroscience terms across 13 459 neuroimaging publications.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data used in the NeuroQuery model.

claim: NeuroQuery uses a multivariate model that predicts the spatial distribution of neurological observations given text describing an experiment, cognitive process, or disease.
source: Our multivariate model predicts the spatial distribution of neurological observations, given text describing an experiment, cognitive process, or disease.
evidence: This describes the core functionality of the NeuroQuery model as designed by the authors.

claim: NeuroQuery can handle text of arbitrary length and terms that are too rare for standard meta-analysis.
source: This approach handles text of arbitrary length and terms that are too rare for standard meta-analysis.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the NeuroQuery model based on its design.

claim: Coordinate-Based Meta-Analysis (CBMA) methods assess the consistency of results across studies by comparing the observed spatial density of reported brain stereotactic coordinates to the null hypothesis of a uniform distribution.
source: Coordinate-Based Meta-Analysis (CBMA) methods (Laird et al., 2005; Wager et al., 2007; Eickhoff et al., 2009) assess the consistency of results across studies, comparing the observed spatial density of reported brain stereotactic coordinates to the null hypothesis of a uniform distribution.
evidence: This describes the methodology of CBMA with citations to relevant literature.

claim: NeuroSynth enables large-scale analyses of brain-imaging studies.
source: Automating CBMA methods across the literature, as in NeuroSynth (Yarkoni et al., 2011), enables large-scale analyses of brain-imaging studies, giving excellent statistical power.
evidence: This is a statement about NeuroSynth's capabilities, supported by citation to Yarkoni et al., 2011.

claim: Closely related terms can lead to markedly different meta-analyses.
source: But closely related terms can lead to markedly different meta-analyses (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1, which shows different results for related terms.

claim: The lack of a universally established vocabulary or ontology to describe mental processes and disorders is a strong impediment to meta-analysis.
source: The lack of a universally established vocabulary or ontology to describe mental processes and disorders is a strong impediment to meta-analysis (Poldrack and Yarkoni, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poldrack and Yarkoni, 2016.

claim: NeuroQuery is a new meta-analysis tool that predicts the neural correlates of neuroscience concepts.
source: We introduce a new meta-analysis tool, NeuroQuery, that predicts the neural correlates of neuroscience concepts – related to behavior, diseases, or anatomy.
evidence: This is a direct description of the NeuroQuery tool developed by the authors.

claim: NeuroQuery considers terms not in isolation, but in a dynamic, contextually-informed way that allows for mutual interactions.
source: To do so, it considers terms not in isolation, but in a dynamic, contextually-informed way that allows for mutual interactions.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery produces high-quality brain maps for concepts studied infrequently in the literature.
source: As a result, NeuroQuery produces high-quality brain maps for concepts studied infrequently in the literature and for a larger class of queries than existing tools – including, for example free text descriptions of a hypothetical experiment.
evidence: This is a claim about the performance of NeuroQuery, which is evaluated in the results section.

claim: NeuroQuery maps do not control a voxel-level null hypothesis.
source: Yet, unlike with conventional meta-analysis, they do not control a voxel-level null hypothesis, hence are less suited to asserting that a particular area is activated in studies, for example of prosopagnosia.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical properties of NeuroQuery maps compared to conventional meta-analysis.

claim: NeuroQuery uses a multivariate model of the statistical link between multiple terms and corresponding brain locations.
source: NeuroQuery uses a multivariate model of the statistical link between multiple terms and corresponding brain locations.
evidence: This describes the statistical model underlying NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery is fitted using supervised machine learning on 13,459 full-text publications.
source: It is fitted using supervised machine learning on 13459 full-text publications.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training data and method used for NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery can predict a brain map given any combination of terms related to neuroscience.
source: It can predict a brain map given any combination of terms related to neuroscience – not only single words, but also detailed descriptions, abstracts, or full papers.
evidence: This describes the input flexibility of the NeuroQuery model.

claim: NeuroQuery uses techniques from natural language processing to infer semantic similarities across terms used in the literature.
source: Using techniques from natural language processing, NeuroQuery infers semantic similarities across terms used in the literature.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in NeuroQuery for handling semantic relationships.

claim: NeuroQuery can recover biologically plausible brain maps where other automated methods lack statistical power.
source: Thus, it makes better use of the available information, and can recover biologically plausible brain maps where other automated methods lack statistical power, for example with terms that are used in few studies, as shown in Section 'NeuroQuery can map rare or difficult concepts'.
evidence: This claim is supported by results presented in a later section of the manuscript.

claim: NeuroQuery is easily usable online at neuroquery.org.
source: NeuroQuery is easily usable online, at neuroquery.org, and the data and source code can be freely downloaded.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of the NeuroQuery tool.

claim: The NeuroQuery model uses an estimate of the relatedness of terms in the vocabulary derived from co-occurrence statistics.
source: The main components of the NeuroQuery model are an estimate of the relatedness of terms in the vocabulary, derived from co-occurrence statistics, and a regression model that links term occurrences to neural activations using supervised machine learning techniques.
evidence: This describes the components of the NeuroQuery statistical model.

claim: NeuroQuery uses a linear regression model to transform term representations into brain maps.
source: Then, it transforms the resulting representation into a brain map using a linear regression model (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the methodology of NeuroQuery, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: NeuroQuery maps are predictions of the likelihood of observation brain location rescaled by their standard deviation.
source: The maps it outputs are predictions of the likelihood of observation brain location (rescaled by their standard deviation).
evidence: This describes the nature of the output from the NeuroQuery model.

claim: NeuroQuery maps do not have the same meaning as ALE, MKDA or NeuroSynth maps as they do not show a voxel-level test statistic.
source: They do not have the same meaning as ALE, MKDA or NeuroSynth maps as they do not show a voxel-level test statistic.
evidence: This is a comparison of NeuroQuery outputs with other meta-analysis methods.

claim: The NeuroQuery corpus contains 13,459 full-text neuroimaging publications.
source: NeuroQuery relies on a corpus of 13459 full-text neuroimaging publications, described in Section 'Building the NeuroQuery training data'.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the size of the corpus used.

claim: The NeuroQuery corpus is the largest of its kind.
source: This corpus is by far the largest of its kind; the NeuroSynth corpus contains a similar number of documents, but uses only the article abstracts, and not the full article texts.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about corpus size, which can be verified by comparing with other available corpora.

claim: NeuroQuery represents the text of a document with Term Frequency · Inverse Document Frequency (TFIDF) features.
source: We represent the text of a document with the (weighted) occurrence frequencies of each phrase from a fixed vocabulary, that is Term Frequency · Inverse Document Frequency (TFIDF) features (Salton and Buckley, 1988).
evidence: This describes the text representation method used in NeuroQuery, with citation to the original TFIDF paper.

claim: The NeuroQuery vocabulary comprises 7,547 terms or phrases related to neuroscience that occur in at least 0.05% of publications.
source: It comprises 7547 terms or phrases related to neuroscience that occur in at least 0.05% of publications.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the vocabulary size and selection criteria.

claim: NeuroQuery automatically extracts 418,772 peak activation coordinates from publications.
source: We automatically extract 418772 peak activations coordinates from publications, and transform them to brain maps with a kernel density estimator.
evidence: This is a statement about the coordinate extraction process and the number of coordinates extracted.

claim: Term co-occurrences are more consistent and reliable than peak activation coordinates and capture semantic relationships.
source: Term co-occurrences, on the other hand, are more consistent and reliable, and capture semantic relationships (Turney and Pantel, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turney and Pantel, 2010.

claim: NeuroQuery uses Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to compute a low-rank approximation of word co-occurrences.
source: Using Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), we compute a low-rank approximation of word co-occurrences (the covariance of the TFIDF features), and obtain a denoised semantic relatedness matrix (details are provided in Section 'smoothing: regularization at test time').
evidence: This describes the method used for semantic smoothing in NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery's text-to-brain encoding model uses linear regression to map text onto brain activations.
source: When analyzing the literature, we fit a linear regression to reliably map text onto brain activations.
evidence: This describes the regression approach used in NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery's model is an additive one across term occurrences.
source: This model is an additive one across the term occurrences, as opposed to logical operations traditionally used to select studies for meta-analysis.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and contrasts it with traditional methods.

claim: NeuroQuery uses a reweighted ridge regression and feature selection procedure to prevent uninformative terms from degrading performance.
source: We use a reweighted ridge regression and feature selection procedure (described in Section 'reweighted ridge matrix and feature (vocabulary) selection') to prevent uninformative terms such as 'magnetoencephalography' from degrading performance.
evidence: This describes the regularization approach used in NeuroQuery.

claim: The feature selection procedure automatically selects around 200 keywords that display a strong statistical link with brain activity.
source: This procedure automatically selects around 200 keywords that display a strong statistical link with brain activity and adapts the regularization applied to each feature.
evidence: This is a statement about the outcome of the feature selection procedure.

claim: NeuroQuery reports a map of Z statistics.
source: In addition, NeuroQuery uses an estimate of the voxel-level variance of association (see methodological details in Section 'Mathematical details of the NeuroQuery statistical model'), and reports a map of Z statistics.
evidence: This describes the output format of NeuroQuery predictions.

claim: NeuroQuery maps cannot be thresholded to reject any simple null hypothesis.
source: Therefore, the resulting map cannot be thresholded to reject any simple null hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical interpretation of NeuroQuery maps.

claim: NeuroQuery maps have a different meaning and different uses than standard meta-analysis maps obtained with ALE.
source: NeuroQuery maps have a different meaning and different uses than standard meta-analysis maps obtained e.g. with ALE.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the interpretation of different types of meta-analysis maps.

claim: NeuroQuery can obtain a brain map directly from a contrast description without manual intervention.
source: The NeuroQuery map was obtained directly from the contrast description in the dataset's documentation, without needing to manually select studies for the meta-analysis nor convert this description to a string pattern usable by existing automatic meta-analysis tools.
evidence: This describes the capability of NeuroQuery as demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: With only 29 matching studies, ALE lacks statistical power for the contrast description 'Read pseudo-words vs. consonant strings'.
source: With only 29 matching studies, ALE lacks statistical power for this contrast description.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of ALE for this specific query, based on the number of matching studies.

claim: NeuroQuery can give good brain maps on combinations of terms that have never been studied together.
source: To study the predictions of NeuroQuery, we first demonstrate that it can indeed give good brain maps on combinations of terms that have never been studied together.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The extrapolation from two terms to their combination is possible thanks to the linear additive model.
source: The extrapolation from two terms for which the model has seen studies, 'distance' and 'color', to their combination, for which the model has no data, is possible thanks to the linear additive model, combining regression maps for 'distance' and 'color'.
evidence: This explains the mechanism by which NeuroQuery can generalize to unseen term combinations.

claim: Measures of how well predictions match the literature decrease only slightly for studies with terms already seen together compared to studies with terms never seen jointly.
source: We find that measures of how well predictions match the literature decrease only slightly for studies with terms already seen together compared to studies with terms never seen jointly (details in Section 'NeuroQuery performance on unseen pairs of terms').
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experiments on unseen term pairs.

claim: For 1,000 pairs of terms, the median correlation between the predicted map for the unseen combination and the meta-analytic map obtained on left-out studies is 0.85.
source: We find a median correlation of 0.85 which shows that the excellent performance observed on Figure 4 is not due to a specific choice of terms.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments on unseen term pairs.

claim: GCLDA is the only multivariate meta-analytic model to date.
source: GCLDA is an important baseline because it is the only multivariate meta-analytic model to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the uniqueness of GCLDA in the field of meta-analysis.

claim: GCLDA produces maps with low spatial resolution because it models brain activations as a mixture of Gaussians.
source: However, it produces maps with a low spatial resolution because it models brain activations as a mixture of Gaussians.
evidence: This is a characterization of GCLDA's limitations based on its modeling approach.

claim: GCLDA takes several days to train and a dozen seconds to produce a map at test time.
source: Moreover, it takes several days to train and a dozen of seconds to produce a map at test time, and is thus unsuitable to build an online and responsive tool like NeuroSynth or NeuroQuery.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational requirements of GCLDA.

claim: By combining term similarities and an additive encoding model, NeuroQuery can accurately map rare or difficult terms for which standard meta-analysis lacks statistical power.
source: By combining term similarities and an additive encoding model, NeuroQuery can accurately map rare or difficult terms for which standard meta-analysis lacks statistical power, as visible on Figure 5.
evidence: This claim is supported by results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Document frequencies roughly follow a power law, meaning that most words are very rare.
source: Document frequencies roughly follow a power law (Piantadosi, 2014), meaning that most words are very rare – half the terms in our vocabulary occur in less than 76 articles (see Section 'Word occurrence frequencies across the corpus').
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piantadosi, 2014 and data about term frequencies in the corpus.

claim: NeuroQuery only needs a dozen examples to produce maps that are qualitatively and quantitatively close to the maps it obtains for the full corpus for many terms.
source: For many terms, NeuroQuery only needs a dozen examples to produce maps that are qualitatively and quantitatively close to the maps it obtains for the full corpus – and to NeuroSynth's full-corpus maps.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: NeuroSynth typically needs hundreds of examples to obtain results similar to those from the full corpus.
source: NeuroSynth typically needs hundreds of examples to obtain similar results, as seen in Figure 6.
evidence: This claim is supported by results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Reducing the number of studies required to map well a term greatly widens the vocabulary that can be studied by meta-analysis.
source: Reducing the number of studies required to map well a term (a.k.a. the sample complexity of the meta-analysis model) therefore greatly widens the vocabulary that can be studied by meta-analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that most terms are rare and NeuroQuery requires fewer examples.

claim: Capturing relations between terms is important because the literature does not use a perfectly consistent terminology.
source: Capturing relations between terms is important because the literature does not use a perfectly consistent terminology.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of semantic modeling based on observed variability in terminology.

claim: Controlled vocabularies tend to have low coverage.
source: The standard solution is to use expert-built ontologies (Poldrack and Yarkoni, 2016), but these tend to have low coverage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Ontologies are typically incomplete in listing relations across terms.
source: In addition, ontologies are typically even more incomplete in listing relations across terms.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of ontologies based on general knowledge of their construction.

claim: NeuroQuery relies on distributional semantics and co-occurrence statistics across the literature to estimate relatedness between terms.
source: Rather than ontologies, NeuroQuery relies on distributional semantics and co-occurrence statistics across the literature to estimate relatedness between terms.
evidence: This describes the approach used in NeuroQuery for modeling semantic relationships.

claim: Continuous semantic links provide robustness to inconsistent terminology.
source: These continuous semantic links provide robustness to inconsistent terminology: consistent meta-analytic maps for similar terms.
evidence: This is a claim about the benefit of the semantic smoothing approach, supported by examples in Figure 1.

claim: Working with the full text of publications associates many more studies to a query than using abstracts.
source: Another reason is that working with the full text of publications associates many more studies to a query: 2779 for 'color', while NeuroSynth matches only 236 abstracts, and 147 for 'huntington', a term not known to NeuroSynth.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of study matching between full-text and abstract-based approaches.

claim: NeuroQuery is a predictive model that can produce brain maps for out-of-sample neuroimaging studies.
source: Unlike standard meta-analysis methods, which compute in-sample summary statistics, NeuroQuery is a predictive model, that can produce brain maps for out-of-sample neuroimaging studies.
evidence: This describes the nature of NeuroQuery as a predictive model.

claim: NeuroQuery captures reliable links from concepts to brain activity that generalize to new, unseen neuroimaging studies.
source: Here we check that NeuroQuery captures reliable links from concepts to brain activity – associations that generalize to new, unseen neuroimaging studies.
evidence: This claim is evaluated through cross-validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: NeuroSynth does not perform well for encoding full documents because it is designed for single-phrase meta-analysis.
source: NeuroSynth does not perform well for this test. Indeed, the NeuroSynth model is designed for single-phrase meta-analysis, and does not have a mechanism to combine words and encode a full document.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of NeuroSynth based on its design.

claim: GCLDA performs significantly better than chance but worse than a simple ridge regression baseline.
source: GCLDA performs significantly better than chance, but still worse than a simple ridge regression baseline.
evidence: This is a comparative performance claim based on experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: More than 72% of the time, NeuroQuery's output has a higher Pearson correlation with the correct map than with a negative example.
source: More than 72% of the time, NeuroQuery's output has a higher Pearson correlation with the correct map than with the negative example (see Figure 7 right).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the encoding prediction experiment.

claim: Peak coordinates reported in the literature are noisy and incomplete with respect to the full activation maps.
source: However, the scores are difficult to interpret, as peak coordinates reported in the literature are noisy and incomplete with respect to the full activation maps.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of using peak coordinates as ground truth.

claim: NeuroQuery predictions match well the IBMA results, with a median Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.80.
source: NeuroQuery predictions match well the IBMA results, with a median Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.80.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with BrainPedia IBMA maps.

claim: Manually reformulating the labels to terms from NeuroSynth's vocabulary gives a median AUC of 0.83 for NeuroSynth and 0.88 for NeuroQuery.
source: Manually reformulating the labels to terms from NeuroSynth's vocabulary gives a median AUC of .83 for NeuroSynth, and also raises the AUC to .88 for NeuroQuery (details in Section 'Comparison with the BrainPedia IBMA study' and Figure 13).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with BrainPedia IBMA maps using reformulated labels.

claim: Both NeuroSynth and NeuroQuery produce maps that are close to the Harvard-Oxford anatomical atlas regions, with a median AUC of 0.98 for NeuroQuery and 0.95 for NeuroSynth.
source: Both NeuroSynth and NeuroQuery produce maps that are close to the atlases' manually segmented regions, with a median AUC of 0.98 for NeuroQuery and 0.95 for NeuroSynth, for the region labels that are present in NeuroSynth's vocabulary.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with anatomical atlas regions.

claim: NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth maps for well-captured terms are very similar, with a median AUC of 0.90.
source: We compare NeuroQuery predictions to NeuroSynth activations by computing the AUC. NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth maps for these well-captured terms are very similar, with a median AUC of 0.90.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with NeuroSynth on terms with strong activations.

claim: NeuroQuery is available as an open-source Python package that can be easily installed on all platforms.
source: NeuroQuery is also available as an open-source Python package that can be easily installed on all platforms: https://github.com/neuroquery/neuroquery (copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/neuroquery).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of the NeuroQuery software.

claim: All the resources used to build NeuroQuery are freely available at https://github.com/neuroquery/neuroquery_data.
source: Finally, all the resources used to build NeuroQuery are freely available at https://github.com/neuroquery/neuroquery_data (copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/neuroquery_data).
evidence: This is a factual statement about data availability.

claim: The NeuroQuery corpus is significantly richer than NeuroSynth.
source: The corpus is significantly richer than NeuroSynth, the largest corpus to date (see Table 3 for a comparison), and manual quality assurance reveals more accurate extraction of brain coordinates (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparisons shown in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: NeuroQuery departs from existing meta-analytic frameworks by treating meta-analysis as a prediction problem.
source: For this, it departs from existing meta-analytic frameworks by treating meta-analysis as a prediction problem.
evidence: This describes the conceptual difference between NeuroQuery and traditional meta-analysis.

claim: NeuroQuery describes neuroscience concepts of interest by continuous combinations of terms rather than matching publications for exact terms.
source: It describes neuroscience concepts of interest by continuous combinations of terms rather than matching publications for exact terms.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery extends the scope of meta-analysis in neuroimaging by combining multiple terms and interpolating between available studies.
source: As it combines multiple terms and interpolates between available studies, it extends the scope of meta-analysis in neuroimaging.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of NeuroQuery compared to traditional methods.

claim: NeuroQuery can capture information for concepts studied much less frequently than those covered by current automated meta-analytic approaches.
source: In particular, it can capture information for concepts studied much less frequently than those that are covered by current automated meta-analytic approaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments on rare terms shown in the results section.

claim: Brainmap was the first systematic database of brain coordinates.
source: Brainmap (Laird et al., 2005) was the first systematic database of brain coordinates.
evidence: This is a historical statement about Brainmap, supported by citation.

claim: NeuroSynth pioneered automated meta-analysis using abstracts from the literature.
source: NeuroSynth (Yarkoni et al., 2011) pioneered automated meta-analysis using abstracts from the literature, broadening a lot the set of terms for which the consistency of reported locations can be tested.
evidence: This is a statement about NeuroSynth's contribution to the field, supported by citation.

claim: Nielsen et al. (2004) used non-negative matrix factorization on the matrix of occurrences of terms for each brain location to extract seven spatial networks associated with cognitive topics.
source: Nielsen et al. (2004) used a non-negative matrix factorization on the matrix of occurrences of terms for each brain location (voxel): their model outputs a set of seven spatial networks associated with cognitive topics, described as weighted combinations of terms.
evidence: This describes prior work by Nielsen et al., supported by citation.

claim: Poldrack et al. (2012) used topic models on the full text of 5,800 publications to extract 130 topics on mental function and disorders.
source: Poldrack et al. (2012) used topic models on the full text of 5800 publications to extract from term cooccurrences 130 topics on mental function and disorders, followed by a classic meta-analysis to map their neural correlates in the literature.
evidence: This describes prior work by Poldrack et al., supported by citation.

claim: The supervised learning used in NeuroQuery differs from that used in Yarkoni et al. (2011) as the latter is a decoding model.
source: In this sense, the supervised learning used in NeuroQuery differs from that used in Yarkoni et al. (2011) : the latter is a decoding model that, given brain locations in a study, predicts the likelihood of neuroscience terms without using relationships between terms.
evidence: This is a comparison of NeuroQuery with prior work, supported by citation.

claim: NeuroQuery will be most successfully used to produce hypotheses and as an exploratory tool.
source: Rather, NeuroQuery will be most successfully used to produce hypotheses and as an exploratory tool, to be confronted with other sources of evidence.
evidence: This is a recommendation about how to use NeuroQuery based on its design and limitations.

claim: NeuroQuery does not provide conclusive evidence that a brain region is recruited by a mental process or affected by a pathology.
source: What NeuroQuery does not do is provide conclusive evidence that a brain region is recruited by a mental process or affected by a pathology.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery is particularly beneficial when the term of interest is rare, when the concept is best described by multiple terms, and when a fully automated method is necessary.
source: Compared to traditional meta-analysis tools, NeuroQuery is particularly beneficial (i) when the term of interest is rare, (ii) when the concept of interest is best described by a combination of multiple terms, and (iii) when a fully automated method is necessary and queries would otherwise need cumbersome manual curation to be understood by other tools.
evidence: This is a statement about the use cases where NeuroQuery provides advantages.

claim: For 'agnosia', the NeuroQuery prediction is driven by indirect associations and focuses on the visual system.
source: In this specific case, the indirect association is problematic because 'agnosia' is not a selected term that NeuroQuery can map by itself, as it is not well-represented in the source data. As a result, the NeuroQuery prediction for 'agnosia' is driven by indirect associations, and focuses on the visual system, rather than areas related to, for example auditory agnosia.
evidence: This is an example of a limitation of NeuroQuery for a specific term.

claim: For 'ADHD', the model builds its prediction on terms that are distant from the query and produces a misleading map.
source: Hence, for 'ADHD', the model builds its prediction on terms that are distant from the query, and produces a misleading map that highlights mostly the cerebellum (https://neuroquery.org/query?text=adhd).
evidence: This is an example of a failure case for NeuroQuery.

claim: The NeuroQuery interface reports failures with a warning stating that results may not be reliable.
source: While this result is not satisfying, the failure is detected by the NeuroQuery interface and reported with a warning stating that results may not be reliable.
evidence: This describes a feature of the NeuroQuery interface for handling failure cases.

claim: The additive combination model is not unique to NeuroQuery and lies at the heart of functional neuroimaging.
source: This model is not unique to NeuroQuery, and lies at the heart of functional neuroimaging, which builds upon the hypothesis of pure insertion of cognitive processes (Ulrich et al., 1999; Poldrack, 2010).
evidence: This contextualizes the additive model used in NeuroQuery within the broader field, supported by citations.

claim: Meta-analyses have little or no ability to correct biases present in the primary literature.
source: First, meta-analyses have little or no ability to correct biases present in the primary literature (e.g., perhaps confirmation bias drives researchers to overreport amygdala activation in emotion studies).
evidence: This is a general statement about limitations of meta-analysis.

claim: Claims that a structure is selective to a mental condition need an explicit statistical model of reverse inference.
source: However, claims that a structure is selective to a mental condition need an explicit statistical model of reverse inference (Wager et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about requirements for making selectivity claims, supported by citation.

claim: The most important confound for reverse inferences in meta-analysis is that some brain locations are reported for many different conditions.
source: In a meta-analysis, the most important confound for reverse inferences is that some brain locations are reported for many different conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about a methodological challenge in meta-analysis.

claim: NeuroQuery accounts for varying baseline across the brain by fitting an intercept and reporting only differences from the baseline.
source: NeuroQuery accounts for this varying baseline across the brain by fitting an intercept and reporting only differences from the baseline.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of NeuroQuery.

claim: Minor variations in task design for finger tapping lead to reproducible variations in neural responses.
source: Indeed, even for a task as simple as finger tapping, minor variations in task design lead to reproducible variations in neural responses (Witt et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Witt et al., 2008.

claim: NeuroQuery grounds meta-analysis in the full-text descriptions of the studies.
source: Rather, NeuroQuery grounds meta-analysis in the full-text descriptions of the studies, which in our view provide the best available proxy for such an idealized ontology.
evidence: This describes the approach taken by NeuroQuery to handle the lack of a complete ontology.

claim: NeuroSynth took a huge step by enabling anyone to perform a fully automated meta-analysis across thousands of studies in a few seconds.
source: NeuroSynth took a huge step in this direction by enabling anyone to perform, in a few seconds, a fully automated meta-analysis across thousands of studies, for an important number of isolated terms.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of NeuroSynth to the field.

claim: NeuroQuery provides statistical maps for arbitrary queries from seldom-studied terms to free-text descriptions of experimental protocols.
source: NeuroQuery provides statistical maps for arbitrary queries – from seldom-studied terms to free-text descriptions of experimental protocols.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of NeuroQuery.

claim: NeuroQuery enables applying fully-automated and quantitative meta-analysis in situations where only semi-manual and subjective solutions were available.
source: Thus, it enables applying fully-automated and quantitative meta-analysis in situations where only semi-manual and subjective solutions were available.
evidence: This is a claim about the advancement provided by NeuroQuery.

claim: The NeuroQuery dataset was collected by downloading around 149,000 full-text journal articles from PubMed Central and Elsevier APIs.
source: We downloaded around 149000 full-text journal articles related to neuroimaging from the PubMed Central (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK25501/) (Sayers, 2009) and Elsevier (https://dev.elsevier.com/api_docs.html) APIs.
evidence: This describes the data collection process for NeuroQuery.

claim: The NeuroQuery dataset contains studies mostly based on fMRI experiments, but also includes PET or structural MRI studies.
source: The resulting studies are mostly based on fMRI experiments, but the dataset also contains Positron Emission Tomography (PET) or structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies.
evidence: This describes the composition of the NeuroQuery dataset.

claim: Out of 149,000 downloaded and formatted articles, 13,459 contain coordinates that could be extracted.
source: Out of the 149000 downloaded and formatted articles, 13459 contain coordinates that could be extracted by this process, resulting in a total of 418772 locations.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the coordinate extraction results.

claim: All extracted coordinates are treated as coordinates in the MNI space, even though some articles refer to the Talairach space.
source: All the extracted coordinates are treated as coordinates in the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space, even though some articles still refer to the Talairach space.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the coordinate extraction process.

claim: Differences between the Talairach and MNI coordinate systems are at most of the order of 1 cm.
source: However, differences between the two coordinate systems are at most of the order of 1 cm, and much smaller in most of the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the magnitude of differences between coordinate systems.

claim: Out of 8,692 articles in the intersection of NeuroSynth and NeuroQuery corpora, the extracted coordinates differ in 1,961 articles (23%).
source: Out of 8692 articles in the intersection of both corpora, the extracted coordinates differ (for at least one coordinate) in 1961 (i.e. in 23% of articles).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of coordinate extraction between NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth.

claim: NeuroQuery's coordinate extraction method extracted false coordinates from 3 out of 40 manually annotated articles, compared to 20 for NeuroSynth.
source: As shown in Table 2, our method extracted false coordinates from fewer articles: 3/40 articles have at least one false location in our dataset, against 20 for NeuroSynth.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from manual evaluation of coordinate extraction.

claim: NeuroQuery uses Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation with a bandwidth yielding a FWHM close to 9 mm.
source: We then use Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 2015) to estimate the density of these activations over the brain. The chosen bandwidth of the Gaussian kernel yields a Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) close to 9 mm, which is in the range of smoothing kernels that are typically used for fMRI meta-analysis (Wager et al., 2007; Wager et al., 2004; Turkeltaub et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the density estimation method used in NeuroQuery, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: NeuroSynth uses a hard ball of 10 mm radius for density estimation.
source: For comparison, NeuroSynth uses a hard ball of 10 mm radius.
evidence: This is a comparison of density estimation methods between NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth.

claim: The NeuroQuery vocabulary is built from the union of terms from several ontologies and labels from 12 anatomical atlases.
source: This vocabulary is built from the union of terms from several ontologies (shown in Table 1) and labels from 12 anatomical atlases (listed in Table 4 in Section 'The choice of vocabulary').
evidence: This describes the sources used to construct the NeuroQuery vocabulary.

claim: TFIDF representations are simple and efficient for many text classification and retrieval applications.
source: These simple representations are popular in document retrieval and text classification because they are very efficient for many applications.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of TFIDF features based on general knowledge in natural language processing.

claim: The NeuroQuery corpus contains over 418,000 peak activation coordinates for more than 13,500 articles.
source: Over 418K peak activation coordinates for more than 13.5K articles.
evidence: This is a summary statistic about the NeuroQuery dataset.

claim: The NeuroQuery vocabulary contains 7,547 terms related to neuroscience, each occurring in at least six articles from which coordinates were extracted.
source: A vocabulary of 7547 terms related to neuroscience, each occurring in at least six articles from which we extracted coordinates.
evidence: This describes the vocabulary used in NeuroQuery.

claim: The NeuroQuery dataset is the largest of its kind.
source: This dataset is the largest of its kind.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about the size of the NeuroQuery dataset.

claim: In terms of raw amount of text, the NeuroQuery corpus is 20 times larger than NeuroSynth's.
source: In terms of raw amount of text, this corpus is 20 times larger than NeuroSynth's.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of corpus sizes.

claim: The NeuroQuery corpus yields over 5.5 million occurrences of a unique term in an article, over five times more than NeuroSynth.
source: Combined with our vocabulary, it yields over 5.5M occurrences of a unique term in an article. This is over five times more than the word occurrence counts distributed by NeuroSynth (https://github.com/neurosynth/neurosynth-data).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of term-study associations.

claim: When considering only terms in NeuroSynth's vocabulary, the NeuroQuery corpus contains over 3 million term-study associations, 4.6 times more than NeuroSynth.
source: When considering only terms in NeuroSynth's vocabulary, the corpus still contains over 3M term-study associations, 4.6 times more than NeuroSynth.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison controlling for vocabulary differences.

claim: There is an important overlap between NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth datasets: 8,692 studies are present in both.
source: There is an important overlap between the selected studies: 8 692 studies are present in both datasets – the Intersection Over Union is 0.45.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of dataset overlap.

claim: The NeuroQuery coordinate extraction set is almost the size of NeuroSynth's, which is 7% larger with 448,255 coordinates.
source: The set of extracted coordinates is almost the size of NeuroSynth's (which is 7% larger with 448255 coordinates after removing duplicates), and is less noisy.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of coordinate extraction results.

claim: Compared with NeuroSynth, NeuroQuery's extraction method reduced the number of articles with incorrect coordinates by a factor of 7.
source: Compared with NeuroSynth, NeuroQuery's extraction method reduced the number of articles with incorrect coordinates (false positives) by a factor of 7, and the number of articles with missing coordinates (false negatives) by a factor of 3 (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of coordinate extraction accuracy.

claim: The most informative words in ridge regression are associated with large coefficients for many voxels.
source: Our approach is based on the observation that when fitting a ridge regression with a uniform regularization, the most informative words are associated with large coefficients for many voxels.
evidence: This is an observation that motivates the feature selection approach.

claim: The feature selection keeps approximately 200 features.
source: In practice, the feature selection keeps u ≈ 200 features.
evidence: This is a statement about the outcome of the feature selection procedure.

claim: The feature selection has a very low computational cost compared to other feature selection schemes.
source: It has a very low computational cost compared to other feature selection schemes.
evidence: This is a claim about the computational efficiency of the feature selection method.

claim: The NeuroQuery model is not very sensitive to the NMF hyperparameters.
source: We find that the NeuroQuery model as a whole is not very sensitive to these hyperparameters and we obtain similar results for a range of different values.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the model to hyperparameter choices.
